newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - Distillate surplus seen again in APIs.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Distillate surplus seen again in APIs.

text.p: Tuesday evening's oil inventory report from the American Petroleum Institute (API) is expected to show a distillate stock surplus for the second consecutive week with little market reaction, dealers said.
"Tonight's expectations are probably already factored in the market. The surprise would be if the APIs were bullish," said John Saucer, analyst with Smith Barney in Houston.
Dealers are expecting distillate stocks to fall 1.5 to 3.5 million barrels. An eight million barrel decline last year at this time creates a year-over-year surplus.

Distillate stocks are comprised of heating oil and diesel. These stocks usually decline in February due to seasonal refinery maintenance and a shift in output toward gasoline ahead of the summer driving season.
Distillate stock declines this year have been tempered by seasonally mild temperatures in the key heating oil market of the northeastern United States, traders said.

The resulting year-over-year stock surplus has accentuated a seasonal downturn in oil prices, stripping five cents a gallon off heating oil prices last week. Gasoline stocks were seen increasing 1.4 to four million barrels.
The rise in west coast stocks accounted for ninety-nine percent of the 6.06 million barrel crude stock build seen for the week ended January 31.
On the other hand, more refiners have joined the winter maintenance cycle, which is expected to depress capacity utilization rates by 0.50 percentage point from 90.3 percent.
With less crude is being used stocks can build up. Moreover, crude imports are expected to increase reflecting an open arbitrage last month from the North Sea.
Tonight's data reflects the week ended February 7.

Although the anticipated stock builds in heating oil and crude may have already been discounted by the market, the sharp drop in oil prices may in themselves cause more stock builds in next several weeks.
Traders said refined product retailers may resist buying new supply while they attempt to de-stock lower priced inventory, preventing stock movement from primary storage which the API data reflects.
